LO1.description: Derive the 2x2 stiffness matrix for a single spring from equilibrium

LO2.description: Explain why diagonal terms are positive and equal to k, and off-diagonal terms are negative

LO3.description: Explain the physical meaning of each column of the stiffness matrix as a unit displacement case

misconceptions.M1: Confusing the element stiffness matrix with the global stiffness matrix
misconceptions.M2: Not understanding why the matrix is singular (thinking it is an error)
misconceptions.M3: Believing the stiffness matrix depends on the applied forces

positive: Starts from or references equilibrium at individual nodes
Discusses direction of spring force on each node
Explains signs of matrix entries through force directions
Notes that columns sum to zero and explains why (overall equilibrium of free body)
Uses 'if I displace this node, the spring does X' reasoning
negative: Writes the matrix directly without derivation
Says 'I remember it is [[k, -k], [-k, k]]'
Justifies signs by 'the pattern' or 'diagonal positive, off-diagonal negative'
Cites the formula f = kx without connecting to nodal forces

LO1.description: Identify the local and global degree of freedom numbering for a given spring system

LO2.description: Construct the connectivity mapping between local element DOFs and global system DOFs

LO3.description: Explain why this mapping is necessary — elements don't know about the global system and the mapping is what connects them

LO4.description: Given a system with N nodes, determine the total number of global DOFs and which elements contribute to each

misconceptions.M1: Thinking that local node 1 must always correspond to the lower-numbered global node
misconceptions.M2: Confusing DOF numbering with physical position (assuming DOF 1 is always the leftmost node)
misconceptions.M3: Not understanding that the same global DOF appears in multiple element stiffness matrices — this is what creates coupling
misconceptions.M4: Believing the connectivity is a property of the element rather than an assignment we make

positive: Explains that each element only knows its local DOFs and the connectivity map translates to the global system
Identifies shared nodes as the mechanism of inter-element communication
Connects the connectivity map to physical attachment (node feels forces from all connected springs)
Explains why the element matrix form is always the same regardless of global position
negative: Writes connectivity maps correctly but cannot explain what they mean physically
Thinks the element stiffness matrix changes depending on its global position
Treats connectivity as a purely bookkeeping exercise without physical significance

LO1.description: Expand an element stiffness matrix from local (2x2) to global size (NxN) using the connectivity map — placing entries in the correct rows and columns

LO2.description: Assemble the global stiffness matrix by summing the expanded element contributions

LO3.description: Explain physically why contributions from different elements add at shared DOFs — forces from multiple springs acting on the same node superpose

LO4.description: Verify properties of the assembled matrix: symmetry, column/row sums equal to zero for the free system, and singularity before boundary conditions

misconceptions.M1: Thinking assembly is concatenation (block diagonal placement) rather than overlapping summation at shared DOFs
misconceptions.M2: Not understanding why shared DOFs accumulate stiffness from multiple elements — treating the overlap as an error or double-counting
misconceptions.M3: Expecting the assembled global matrix to be invertible before applying boundary conditions
misconceptions.M4: Assembling element matrices in the wrong positions because of connectivity map errors

positive: Explains that shared DOFs accumulate stiffness because the node feels forces from all connected elements
Uses superposition reasoning: the force at a node is the sum of contributions from all connected springs
Connects the banded structure of the assembled matrix to the physical connectivity of the system
Explains singularity as rigid body modes of the unsupported system
Verifies the assembly by checking that column sums are zero (free body equilibrium)
negative: Places element matrices without explaining why entries go where they do
Treats assembly as a mechanical procedure without physical interpretation
Says entries 'add up' without explaining why (superposition of forces)
Cannot predict the structure of the assembled matrix before computing it

LO1.description: Apply displacement boundary conditions to the global system by modifying rows and columns using the elimination approach

LO2.description: Explain physically why the unmodified global matrix is singular and why applying BCs makes it invertible — removing rigid body modes by providing a spatial reference

LO3.description: Distinguish between essential (displacement) and natural (force) boundary conditions, and understand that force BCs appear on the right-hand side while displacement BCs modify the left-hand side

LO4.description: Recover reaction forces at constrained DOFs after solving the reduced system

misconceptions.M1: Applying boundary conditions before assembly — modifying element matrices instead of the global system
misconceptions.M2: Confusing force BCs with displacement BCs — trying to impose a known force by modifying the stiffness matrix
misconceptions.M3: Not understanding that the singular matrix is correct and expected before BCs — thinking the assembly went wrong
misconceptions.M4: Forgetting to recover reactions — solving for displacements and stopping
misconceptions.M5: Thinking that applying BCs 'fixes' a broken matrix rather than understanding it removes the physical rigid body freedom

positive: Explains that BCs provide a spatial reference that eliminates rigid body modes
Connects the elimination of rows/columns to physically removing a DOF from the system
Distinguishes between 'this node cannot move' (displacement BC) and 'this node has a known force' (force BC)
Explains reactions as the forces the supports must exert to maintain the prescribed displacement
Understands that the reduced system describes only the free nodes
negative: Applies BCs as a mathematical recipe without physical interpretation
Says 'we delete rows and columns to make the matrix invertible' without explaining why it was singular
Treats reactions as an afterthought rather than a physical quantity of interest
Cannot explain the difference between prescribing a displacement and prescribing a force

LO1.description: Solve the reduced system of equations for the unknown displacements

LO2.description: Back-substitute the computed displacements into the element stiffness equations to recover internal element forces — extension and spring force for each element

LO3.description: Compute reaction forces at the constrained nodes using the full global system

LO4.description: Interpret the signs of displacements, element forces, and reactions physically — direction of movement, tension vs compression, direction of support forces

misconceptions.M1: Stopping after solving for displacements and not recovering element forces or reactions
misconceptions.M2: Confusing element forces with nodal forces — the internal force in a spring is not the same as the external force applied to a node
misconceptions.M3: Sign convention errors when interpreting tension vs compression
misconceptions.M4: Computing reactions incorrectly by using the reduced system instead of the full system
misconceptions.M5: Not checking whether the results make qualitative physical sense before trusting the numbers

positive: Predicts qualitative behavior before solving (which way should each node move, which springs should be in tension)
Distinguishes between displacement solution, element forces, and reactions as three different physical quantities
Interprets signs consistently: displacement direction, tension or compression, reaction direction
Checks the solution against physical intuition as a verification step
negative: Solves the equations and reports numbers without physical interpretation
Cannot explain what a positive or negative displacement means for a specific node
Confuses the force in a spring with the external load at a node
Cannot predict even the qualitative direction of displacements before solving

LO1.description: Verify global equilibrium — confirm that the sum of all external forces (applied loads plus reactions) equals zero

LO2.description: Verify element-level equilibrium — confirm that every node individually satisfies force balance

LO3.description: Predict qualitative behavior before solving and use it to catch errors — which way should nodes move, which springs should be in tension

LO4.description: Identify when results are physically unreasonable and diagnose the likely source of error

misconceptions.M1: Assuming the computed answer is always correct without verification — trusting the math blindly
misconceptions.M2: Not checking units or dimensional consistency
misconceptions.M3: Not being able to predict qualitative behavior before solving — treating FEA as a black box
misconceptions.M4: Thinking that equilibrium checks are optional rather than a professional requirement
misconceptions.M5: Confusing a verification check with a derivation — verification uses an independent path, not repetition

positive: Treats verification as mandatory and non-negotiable
Uses qualitative prediction as an independent check against computed results
Can identify specific error sources when results are unreasonable
Understands that equilibrium must hold at every level: element, node, and global
Recognizes that a correct FEA result must be self-consistent across all levels
negative: Treats verification as an afterthought or academic exercise
Cannot predict even the qualitative direction of displacements
Accepts unreasonable results without questioning them
Only checks global equilibrium and ignores node-level balance
Cannot diagnose the source of an error when results are wrong
